documents.title: Generative AI
documents.summary: A faculty-facing page from the Office of Online Learning that defines generative AI, lists its limitations, privacy risks and detector unreliability, and advises instructors to state their AI rules in the syllabus and to redesign assessments. It sets no student-facing rule and leaves permission to each instructor.
documents.stance_why: The page never says whether students may use AI; it tells faculty to 'inform students whether they are allowed to use Generative AI programs in your class', so the decision is handed to instructors.

units.why: The page defines generative AI as technology that creates 'new and original content', which sets what the guidance covers, so a definition/scope type with informs modality.
units.anchor: Generative AI refers to a type of artificial intelligence technology that is designed to create

units.why: States that tools 'often' produce 'fabricated citations'; a fact warning that output cannot be trusted, which is the verify-output type even though phrased as information.
units.anchor: the references often deviate from the generated content or consist of fabricated citations

units.why: Says responses 'could be inaccurate, excessively simplified, unsophisticated, or influenced by bias'; a warning about output quality and bias, filed under verify-output because it concerns reliability of what AI says.
units.anchor: Potential to generate responses that could be inaccurate, excessively simplified, unsophisticated, or influenced by bias
units.fit_note: Also names bias as a limitation, which P53 would cover as an ethical concern; filed under P31 because the framing is output reliability.

units.why: Directs users to 'exercise caution and critical thinking' and verify with trusted sources: an advisory (should) about checking AI output.
units.anchor: Users should exercise caution and critical thinking when interpreting and relying on its output

units.why: Lists 'Educational Uses' such as concept clarification, writing support and coding assistance without making them rules; it names the benefits/uses of AI for learning, so informs, not a permission.
units.anchor: Research Assistant Language learning Writing support Concept clarification
units.policy: Lists educational uses of generative AI: research assistant, language learning, writing support, concept clarification, creative writing workshops, coding and programming assistance, simulation and role playing, and others.
units.fit_note: A list of possible uses presented as facts; also resembles permitted-use types (P12, P91, P16) but nothing says students may do them.

units.why: Tells instructors to 'Talk to your students about responsible use' that excludes personal information, and notes tools may share data with vendors: a privacy duty for instructors.
units.anchor: Talk to your students about responsible use of the systems that does not include personal
units.policy: Instructors talk to students about responsible use of generative AI systems that does not include personal information.

units.why: The page says tools 'may share personal information collected from the user with third parties' and 'use the information provided to train the system'; a privacy fact.
units.anchor: may share personal information collected from the user with third parties, including vendors

units.why: Encourages instructors to have students read the 'Terms of Agreement and the Privacy Policy' before signing up; separate recommendation from the privacy talk, about terms of use.
units.anchor: encourage them to read the Terms of Agreement and the Privacy Policy
units.policy: Instructors encourage students to read the Terms of Agreement and the Privacy Policy before signing up for any AI tool.
units.fit_note: Terms-of-use reading is advised for privacy reasons rather than copyright or ownership, which P52 mainly covers.

units.why: States detectors 'have a high rate of false positives' and should not be viewed as 'complete solutions': a statement that detectors are unreliable.
units.anchor: many of the tools have a high rate of false positives

units.why: Warns that care 'should be taken to avoid viewing them as complete solutions', advising instructors not to treat detectors as conclusive.
units.anchor: Care should be taken to avoid viewing them as complete solutions.

units.why: The Office 'will not support or endorse any of the products currently available'; an institutional position on detection tools, so it fits do-not-rely-on-detectors.
units.anchor: the Office of Online Learning will not support or endorse any of the products currently

units.why: The Office promises to 'continue to monitor the available tools and will update the campus', a commitment to keep guidance current.
units.anchor: We will continue to monitor the available tools and will update the campus

units.why: Instructs faculty: 'In your syllabus, inform students whether they are allowed to use Generative AI'; a syllabus-statement duty.
units.anchor: In your syllabus, inform students whether they are allowed to use Generative AI programs in

units.why: The page leaves the decision to each instructor ('whether they are allowed ... in your class'), so the permission is set per course, not by one rule.
units.anchor: whether they are allowed to use Generative AI programs in your class
units.policy: Whether students may use generative AI programs in a class, and how and for what purposes, is decided by the instructor and stated in the syllabus.

units.why: Tells instructors to 'Talk to your students about academic integrity and why it matters', which explains the rules beyond listing them.
units.anchor: Talk to your students about academic integrity and why it matters.

units.why: Encourages instructors to have students 'verify that the content generated by the model is a genuine reflection of their knowledge and understanding'; ownership of what is submitted.
units.anchor: verify that the content generated by the model is a genuine reflection of their knowledge
units.policy: Instructors encourage students to verify that the content generated by the model is a genuine reflection of their knowledge and understanding.
units.fit_note: Wording is about reflecting the student's own understanding, near P30 but not 'explain every line'.

units.why: 'Teach students to critically evaluate the information provided by Generative AI' is an instruction to teach output verification.
units.anchor: Teach students to critically evaluate the information provided by Generative AI.

units.why: Says that if instructors allow AI 'here is some information on how to cite it appropriately' (APA and others); recommends citation of allowed AI use.
units.anchor: If you plan on allowing Generative AI use in the classroom, here is some information
units.policy: Where instructors allow generative AI use, AI use is cited appropriately; the page points to APA guidance and other citation formats.

units.why: Recommends to 'reduce the number of high stakes summative assessments and include more frequent, low stakes, more formative assessments' as a response to AI; assessment redesign.
units.anchor: reduce the number of high stakes summative assessments and include more frequent, low stakes, more

units.why: Suggests 'create assignments that are harder to complete with AI (e.g., personal reflections ...)'; redesigning assignments around AI.
units.anchor: create assignments that are harder to complete with AI

units.why: Suggests 'consider flipping the class' so students apply and perform in class; course-structure redesign, with more work done in class.
units.anchor: consider flipping the class where students read materials and view lectures at home

documents.title: Resolution: Syllabus Statement: Use of AI in courses (S-2024-10)
tiers: Students May NOT Use AI Tools
Yes, Students May Use AI Tools
Students Are Fully Encouraged to Use AI Tools
documents.summary: A 2024 Faculty Senate resolution that endorses three optional syllabus statements: no AI, AI permitted with a disclosure statement, and AI fully encouraged with a disclosure statement. It also asks the administration to support faculty training on AI.
documents.stance_why: The Senate 'endorses the following statements for faculty's consideration', offering a prohibit, a permit and an encourage template rather than choosing one, so the stance is delegates with three tiers.

units.why: The resolution 'endorses the following statements for faculty's consideration', three ready-made syllabus statements ranging from no AI to full encouragement, which is a set of named levels.
units.anchor: endorses the following statements for faculty’s consideration
units.policy: The Faculty Senate endorses three syllabus statements: students may not use AI tools, students may use AI tools, and students are fully encouraged to use AI tools.

units.why: Statements are offered 'for faculty's consideration', so each instructor picks one; the Senate does not set the default.
units.anchor: for faculty’s consideration in the incorporation of AI tools into their syllabi
units.policy: Faculty consider the endorsed statements when incorporating AI tools into their syllabi.

units.why: Tier 1 states 'students are not permitted to use AI tools to complete assignments, tests, or any form of coursework submission', a full ban within the course.
units.anchor: students are not permitted to use AI tools to complete assignments, tests, or any form

units.why: Tier 1 gives the reason: 'engage directly with the material and develop their critical thinking, analytical, problem-solving, and writing skills without reliance on external AI assistance', i.e. skill-building.
units.anchor: ensure that students engage directly with the material and develop their critical thinking

units.why: Tier 1 says violations including 'presenting AI-generated content as one's own work, will be considered academic misconduct', linking it to integrity processes.
units.anchor: will be considered academic misconduct and dealt with according to the university's academic integrity guidelines

units.why: Tier 2 says 'students are permitted to use AI tools to assist with their coursework, including research, drafting, and problem-solving'; permission by default for that course.
units.anchor: students are permitted to use AI tools to assist with their coursework, including research, drafting,

units.why: Tier 2 stresses 'it is crucial that students critically evaluate the information and outputs generated by AI tools, ensuring accuracy and relevance'.
units.anchor: it is crucial that students critically evaluate the information and outputs generated by AI tools

units.why: Tier 2 requires that 'All submissions must be accompanied by a statement detailing the extent of AI assistance received', a disclosure with each submission.
units.anchor: All submissions must be accompanied by a statement detailing the extent of AI assistance received

units.why: Tier 2 reminds students to adhere 'to academic integrity policies when using these tools'; defers to existing university rules rather than adding one.
units.anchor: Students are reminded to adhere to academic integrity policies when using these tools
units.policy: Students adhere to academic integrity policies when using AI tools.
units.fit_note: Reminder to follow integrity policies while using permitted AI; P77 is about existing law and policy, not AI-specific rules.

units.why: Tier 2 says work must be 'properly cited'; a citation duty for AI use even when AI is allowed.
units.anchor: ensuring that all work is properly cited
units.policy: Students ensure that all work is properly cited when using AI tools.

units.why: Tier 2 bars presenting 'AI-generated content' as 'their original work', so permitted use still may not be passed off as the student's own.
units.anchor: AI-generated content is not presented as their original work
units.policy: Students ensure that AI-generated content is not presented as their original work.
units.fit_note: Applies to prose and any content, not only code; the rule is about passing off AI output as own.

units.why: Tier 3 says 'Students are encouraged to use AI tools to enhance their learning experience in this course', the strongest positive stance.
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to use AI tools to enhance their learning experience in this course

units.why: Tier 3 names uses: 'brainstorming, researching, and exploring complex concepts'; brainstorming is the main permission.
units.anchor: These tools can assist in brainstorming, researching, and exploring complex concepts.
units.fit_note: Also lists researching and exploring concepts (P12 tutor use), grouped here under P15 for brainstorming.

units.why: Tier 3 frames AI use as 'an opportunity to engage critically with technology, fostering a deeper understanding'; a benefit claim, not a rule.
units.anchor: AI tools should be used as an opportunity to engage critically with technology

units.why: Tier 3 requires 'All submissions must be accompanied by a statement detailing the extent to which AI tools were utilized'; disclosure with each submission.
units.anchor: All submissions must be accompanied by a statement detailing the extent to which AI tools

units.why: Tier 3 again reminds students of integrity policies and 'correctly citing sources', repeated for the encouraged tier.
units.anchor: including correctly citing sources and ensuring that AI-generated content is not presented as their original
units.policy: Students correctly cite sources and ensure that AI-generated content is not presented as their original work.
units.fit_note: Combines citation and not-presenting-as-own in one sentence; filed under P19 (the stricter part).

units.why: A 'Whereas' says AI tools 'have the potential to enhance teaching methodologies, learning experiences, and research capabilities', stating benefits.
units.anchor: tools have the potential to enhance teaching methodologies, learning experiences, and research capabilities

units.why: A 'Whereas' says responsible AI use 'aligns with SCSU's mission to prepare students for the challenges of the modern world', a professional-preparation rationale for permitting AI.
units.anchor: The responsible and ethical use of AI tools aligns with SCSU's mission to prepare students
units.fit_note: Prepares students for the modern world rather than naming employers; closest to P44.

units.why: A 'Whereas' commits SCSU to 'the integration of emerging technologies in the educational process', framing the resolution's purpose.
units.anchor: committed to fostering academic excellence, innovation, and the integration of emerging technologies

units.why: The final resolved clause 'encourages the administration to provide support and resources for faculty training and development in the use of AI tools'.
units.anchor: provide support and resources for faculty training and development in the use of AI tools
units.policy: The Faculty Senate encourages the administration to provide support and resources for faculty training and development in the use of AI tools.

units.why: The same clause asks the administration 'to facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration in the exploration of innovative applications of AI', a faculty-community effort.
units.anchor: facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration in the exploration of innovative applications of AI
units.policy: The Faculty Senate encourages the administration to facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration in the exploration of innovative applications of AI in teaching and research.
units.fit_note: Collaboration among faculty on AI applications in teaching and research, not training; nearest type is faculty support.

documents.title: Resolution: AI-Powered Tools (S-2023-10)
documents.summary: A 2023 Faculty Senate resolution treating unsanctioned AI use, meaning use without the teaching faculty's explicit written consent, as academic misconduct under the BOR/CSCU code. It leaves detailed acceptable-use rules to each instructor's syllabus and lets instructors sanction.
documents.stance_why: The Senate treats 'unsanctioned use of AI-powered tools ... without the explicit written consent of the teaching faculty' as misconduct, so AI is barred unless an instructor permits it in writing, which is restrict.

units.why: The Senate treats use 'without the explicit written consent of the teaching faculty' as a violation, which makes AI barred unless faculty give written permission, a fallback restriction.
units.anchor: without the explicit written consent of the teaching faculty
units.policy: Use of AI-powered tools in the completion of student work is unsanctioned unless the teaching faculty give explicit written consent.
units.fit_note: Also sets a default of no AI when the instructor is silent; P06 chosen over P01 because the key element is the written-consent condition.

units.why: The resolution calls unsanctioned AI use 'a violation of the BOR/CSCU Student Code of Conduct part D.1, and therefore a form of academic misconduct'.
units.anchor: a violation of the BOR/CSCU Student Code of Conduct part D.1, and therefore a form
units.policy: Unsanctioned use of AI-powered tools in the completion of student work is a violation of the BOR/CSCU Student Code of Conduct part D.1 and a form of academic misconduct.

units.why: 'Specific procedures surrounding the acceptable use ... fall within the purview of individual faculty members via their course syllabi' places the detailed rule with instructors.
units.anchor: fall within the purview of individual faculty members via their course syllabi
units.policy: Specific procedures surrounding acceptable use of AI-powered tools in the classroom, virtual learning environment, research and course assignments fall within the purview of individual faculty members via their course syllabi.

units.why: The Senate says the 'Instructor may impose appropriate academic sanctions per the guidelines', stating who sanctions but naming no specific penalty.
units.anchor: the Instructor may impose appropriate academic sanctions per the guidelines outlined in the Faculty Senate
units.fit_note: Gives instructors authority to sanction under existing guidelines but states no concrete penalty, so only partly P37.

units.why: Quotes the code's definition of cheating, 'use of sources beyond those authorized by the instructor', which the resolution relies on to classify AI use as misconduct.
units.anchor: use of sources beyond those authorized by the instructor in writing papers, preparing reports, solving
units.policy: Cheating includes use of sources beyond those authorized by the instructor in writing papers, preparing reports, solving problems or carrying out other assignments.

units.why: Quotes cheating as 'use of any unauthorized assistance in taking quizzes, tests or examinations', the exam clause the resolution builds on.
units.anchor: use of any unauthorized assistance in taking quizzes, tests or examinations
units.policy: Cheating includes use of any unauthorized assistance in taking quizzes, tests or examinations.
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; it is the existing code that the resolution applies to AI.

units.why: 'Academic honesty and integrity represent guiding tenets of SCSU' gives integrity as the reason for the AI resolution.
units.anchor: Academic honesty and integrity represent guiding tenets of SCSU

units.why: The Senate 'supports the continuing work of developing formal policies and procedures' with named offices, so the resolution is a step in an unfinished process.
units.anchor: supports the continuing work of developing formal policies and procedures for SCSU
units.fit_note: Also names the stakeholder bodies involved in drafting (closer to P84), kept under P54 because it is about ongoing development.

units.why: 'The recent rise of AI-powered tools represent a dramatic shift in the academic landscape' and tools 'convincingly simulating human responses' state the concern behind the resolution.
units.anchor: AI-powered tools are capable of convincingly simulating human responses
units.uncovered_note: States as a reason for concern that AI output is hard to tell apart from human work; no type covers the difficulty-of-telling-apart rationale (P82 is about control limits).

documents.title: Academic Honesty
documents.summary: The CS department's Academic Honesty page defines plagiarism and lists generating course evaluation materials with AI-powered tools and submitting them as one's own as an example. The rest is general plagiarism, detection and sanction guidance with no other mention of AI.
documents.stance_why: The only AI sentence says 'Generating CEMS using AI-powered tools and submitting [them] as one's own work' is plagiarism, so AI-produced submissions are banned; no permitted uses are described, so prohibit (narrow, as the page is silent on other AI uses).

units.why: The department lists 'Generating CEMS using AI-powered tools and submitting them as one's own work' as plagiarism, banning AI-produced submissions presented as own.
units.anchor: Generating CEMS using AI-powered tools and submitting thenas one's own work
units.policy: Generating Course Evaluation Materials and Solutions (CEMS) using AI-powered tools and submitting them as one's own work is plagiarism.
units.fit_note: Also classifies the act as plagiarism (P36); filed under P19 because the rule is about not submitting AI-generated work.

units.why: Defines plagiarism as 'presenting, as one's own, the code, ideas, words, or products of another person ... without proper acknowledgment', the base definition the AI example sits in.
units.anchor: presenting, as one's own, the code, ideas, words, or products of another person
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; it is the definition under which the AI example is listed.

units.why: 'Your work should be yours and yours alone' is the department's ownership rule, which applies to AI-assisted work too.
units.anchor: Your work should be yours and yours alone.
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific, but the page's only AI-related rule sits under this heading.

units.why: 'Students may not receive any credit for CEMS not developed by themselves' sets that outside-source material earns no credit.
units.anchor: Students may not receive any credit for CEMS not developed by themselves.
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; limits credit to student-developed work.

units.why: 'If you are not sure ... consult with your instructor before submission' tells students to ask when unsure.
units.anchor: consult with your instructor before submission
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific.

units.why: 'A faculty can employ any computational software and/or manual inspection to conclude that one or more students have plagiarized', allowing any detection method.
units.anchor: A faculty can employ any computational software and/or manual inspection to conclude that one or
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific.

units.why: The faculty must notify students 'in writing according to the SCSU Guidelines', a formal reporting step once plagiarism is detected.
units.anchor: the faculty shall notify the student(s) of the plagiarism case in writing
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; notification of the student is closer to a procedure than to the formal-report type.

units.why: 'The faculty is NOT obligated to tell the student how the case was detected' keeps detection methods undisclosed.
units.anchor: The faculty is NOT obligated to tell the student how the case was detected
units.fit_note: Says nothing about what evidence suffices; it only releases faculty from explaining the detection method.

units.why: Lists sanctions: 'A reduced grade for the assignment', 'A grade of F for the assignment', 'A grade of F for the course', concrete penalties for plagiarism, including AI.
units.anchor: A grade of F for the assignment in question
units.policy: Academic sanctions imposed by the instructor may include a reduced grade for the assignment, the opportunity to revise the assignment, additional course work, a grade of F for the assignment, or a grade of F for the course.
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; a range of sanctions rather than one fixed penalty.

units.why: The page says sanctions 'may be made in consultation with the Office of Student Conduct', setting how the integrity process is run.
units.anchor: this determination may be made in consultation with the Office of Student Conduct
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; consultation is optional.

units.why: 'A student accused of academic dishonesty has the right to appeal an instructor's allegations', which gives students a way to respond.
units.anchor: A student accused of academic dishonesty has the right to appeal an instructor’s allegations.
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; an appeal right, not an initial chance to respond.

units.why: 'The CS department will follow the policies and guidelines developed by the SCSU Faculty Senate' makes the department defer to the Senate, which includes the AI resolutions.
units.anchor: The CS department will follow the policies and guidelines developed by the SCSU Faculty Senate
units.fit_note: Defers to a higher body's policies; it does not mention law or AI.

notes: No school-level policy found; course layer deferred. CS Academic Honesty page has one AI sentence; its general plagiarism, detection and sanction units are coded as P-types but are not AI-specific (marked in fit_note). Source text of the CS page contains the typo 'thenas' (kept in anchor). Topic codes were chosen freely because AGENT_BRIEF.md was not present. Candidate: the 2023 Senate 'AI simulates human responses convincingly' concern is UNCOVERED.
